title: Judges 3:1–6
context: Judges 3 opens by naming the peoples the LORD left in the land after Joshua’s generation died. Chapter 2 has already explained the pattern of the book: Israel forsakes the LORD, is handed over to oppressors, cries out, and is rescued by a judge, only to fall back again. These six verses state two purposes for the remaining nations: to teach war to a generation that had not known the conquest, and to test whether Israel would listen to the commandments given through Moses. The passage closes with a sober report that Israel lived among these peoples, intermarried with them, and served their gods. Both traditions read this as shared ground: God governs the circumstances of his people, he tests their faithfulness, and compromise with idolatry is a real and serious failure. The notes treat the divine testing carefully, without forcing a doctrinal fork onto a narrative about covenant loyalty.

verses.text: Now these are the nations which the LORD left, to test Israel by them, even as many as had not known all the wars of Canaan;
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator names the nations the LORD left in the land and gives the first purpose: to test Israel, especially the generation that had not known the wars of Canaan. The leftover peoples are not an accident of history but part of how God deals with his people after Joshua.

Arminian readers see the testing as genuine, with a real outcome that depends on Israel’s response. God sets his people in circumstances that call for faithful choices, and the story that follows shows that those choices matter and carry real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the LORD left these nations by his own decision, so even Israel’s incomplete conquest lies within his governing providence. Nothing in the land falls outside his purposes.

That does not make Israel’s failures any less their own; chapter 2 has already held them responsible. Both traditions agree that God’s rule over circumstances and the people’s accountability stand together in this verse.

verses.text: only that the generations of the children of Israel might know, to teach them war, at least those who knew nothing of it before:
verses.arminianNotes:
A second purpose is given: that a new generation of Israel might learn war, since they had not experienced it before. The verse runs on from verse 1 and continues into the list that follows, reflecting the WEB’s single long sentence.

Arminian readers see God training a people for faithful action rather than simply acting in their place. The struggles of the new generation become a school in which trust and obedience have to be learned and practiced in real conflict.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the LORD’s purpose here is pedagogical: each generation has to learn for itself the dependence on God that the conquest generation had known firsthand. God’s grace does not pass automatically by inheritance.

Both traditions agree that God works through ordinary hardship to form his people, and that the faith of parents does not replace the need for each new generation to know the LORD and his ways.

verses.text: the five lords of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived on Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal Hermon to the entrance of Hamath.
verses.arminianNotes:
The list names the five lords of the Philistines, the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites of the Lebanon range, from Baal Hermon to the entrance of Hamath. These peoples are spread along the coast and the north, at the edges of Israel’s settlement.

Arminian readers note that these neighbors represent both military threat and spiritual temptation. The list is a map of the pressures Israel will face, and the chapters that follow show these very peoples becoming occasions for either faithfulness or compromise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the list as a reminder that the land was still contested and that God’s promise had not yet been fully realized in Israel’s possession. The geography underscores that the remaining work was real and substantial.

Both traditions agree that the list is descriptive rather than doctrinal, and that it prepares the reader for the stories ahead, especially the long conflict with the Philistines that runs through the later chapters of Judges.

verses.text: They were left to test Israel by them, to know whether they would listen to the LORD’s commandments, which he commanded their fathers by Moses.
verses.arminianNotes:
The verse restates the purpose of the testing: to know whether Israel would listen to the LORD’s commandments given to their fathers through Moses. The test concerns covenant obedience, not military skill alone.

Arminian readers often emphasize that the language of knowing whether describes a real test with a genuinely open outcome from Israel’s side. God engages his people relationally, and their response to his commandments is a meaningful act of loyalty or disloyalty, not a foregone performance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers commonly read the testing as revealing what is in Israel’s heart, bringing their loyalty or disloyalty into the open, rather than supplying God with information he lacked. The same kind of language appears in Deuteronomy 8:2, where the wilderness testing serves a similar purpose.

Both traditions agree that the test is real, that Israel is accountable for how it responds, and that the measure of faithfulness is listening to the commandments the LORD gave through Moses.

verses.text: The children of Israel lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator reports that Israel lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, the familiar list of the land’s earlier inhabitants. Living among them is presented as the setting for the failure that follows.

Arminian readers see the danger of gradual accommodation. Israel did not fall in a single moment; proximity without distinctiveness slowly opened the way to compromise, and each step was a choice that could have gone differently.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the list echoes the nations the LORD had promised to drive out, so the verse quietly measures the distance between the promise and Israel’s present condition. The covenant people now live as neighbors to those they were told to dispossess.

Both traditions agree that the problem is not mere coexistence but the loss of covenant distinctiveness, which the next verse spells out in intermarriage and the worship of other gods.

verses.text: They took their daughters to be their wives, and gave their own daughters to their sons and served their gods.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel intermarried with the peoples of the land and served their gods, exactly what Moses had warned against (Deuteronomy 7:3–4). The sequence from marriage alliances to worship shows how close relationships shaped religious loyalty.

Arminian readers stress Israel’s responsibility here. The people were warned, knew the commandments, and chose a path that led them away from the LORD, which is why the oppression that follows is presented as just and not arbitrary.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in this verse the depth of human inclination to turn from God even after great deliverance. The generation after Joshua does not drift merely by circumstance but by hearts that went after other gods.

Both traditions agree that the concern is idolatry rather than ethnicity, since the Mosaic warning was that such marriages would turn Israel’s heart to serve other gods, and that is exactly what the verse reports.
